summary: llmcord makes exactly one LLM call: a streamed chat.completions request in on_message, against a client built per message from whichever `providers` entry the current /model points at. I wrapped that client construction with the vendored runtime, so requests to api.openai.com whose model is a Router catalog id now go to Router's /v1/responses (request, SSE stream and finish_reason translated back) and everything else -- OpenRouter, Google, xAI, Azure, LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM, and any model not in the catalog -- goes exactly where it did before. Nothing changes until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set. A router.policy.json adds spend labels, a prompt-cache key for provider affinity, and a 90s cap on a silent stream; it deliberately does not pin a service tier, because on this key Flex cost half of standard with no measured latency penalty. Verified against the simulator (the call reaches /v1/responses with the feature label llmcord.py:on_message) and live against Router (gpt-5.5 and gpt-6-luna both streamed back correctly through llmcord's own client).
reviewed: I read the app as its CTO would: one user-waiting streamed call, on a Discord bot whose own system prompt says 'optimize for brevity', configured to run gpt-5.5 at reasoning_effort: high with no output cap, no fallback, no timeout, and a clock ticking at the front of every prompt. I priced the shipped default against cheaper catalog models on real Router traffic, measured what the clock in the prefix costs in lost cache hits, checked every configured model's routing decision, and read the failure paths. Six improvements are built and tested on branches; six more are proposed, the big one being a native port to the Responses API that would unlock per-request fallback timeouts, per-conversation cache keys and cross-vendor web_search.

calls.model: openai/gpt-5.5 (config `models`, first entry; switchable at runtime with /model)

items.title: Route the OpenAI-provider call through Router
items.summary: Wrap the AsyncOpenAI construction in on_message so OpenAI-host requests for catalog models go to Router.
items.gains: One key and one bill across vendors for the bot's OpenAI traffic, per-request spend attribution, the Router levers in router.policy.json, and access to the whole catalog under the existing `openai` provider entry (openai/claude-haiku-5-5 is served by Anthropic with no second api_key).
items.price: no change by itself: the same model serves, at Router's list price, which matched OpenAI's for every call measured.
items.why: llmcord speaks Chat Completions and Router has no /v1/chat/completions endpoint, so pointing the client straight at Router would 404. The runtime under the SDK's HTTP client is the only way to route this app without rewriting its streaming loop; it also decides per request, so the OpenRouter / Ollama / Azure clients built from the same line are untouched.

evidence.detail: A probe reproducing on_message's client construction and streaming kwargs: 1 request reached router-sim, valid, /v1/responses, feature=llmcord.py:on_message, model=gpt-5.5.
Same probe against real Router: gpt-5.5 -> 200, served gpt-5.5-2026-04-23, streamed, finish_reason stop; gpt-6-luna -> 200, 1.5s to first token. Chat-chunk translation and finish_reason both correct.
Routing decisions for all three configured models (ROUTER_MIGRATE_TRACE): openai/gpt-5.5 -> Router; openrouter/~anthropic/claude-opus-latest -> provider; ollama/llama4 -> provider.
2 passed (compileall + import llmcord), same as the baseline.

items.title: router.policy.json: spend labels, cache affinity, stream timeout
items.summary: Adds metadata, prompt_cache_key and provider_timeout to Router-bound requests only.
items.gains: Spend views can attribute this bot's traffic (metadata app/surface); prompt_cache_key gives the provider affinity that makes prefix caching actually hit; provider_timeout ends a stream that has gone silent for 90s instead of leaving a Discord typing indicator up for the SDK's 600s default.
items.price: no change; prompt_cache_key can only reduce cost.
items.why: These are the Router fields that are pure upside for an interactive chat call. I deliberately did not pin service_tier: on this key gpt-6-luna at Flex cost $1.24e-05 against $2.27e-05 at standard for the same prompt, with time-to-first-token of 1.5s vs 1.9s, so the account's Flex default is better for both cost and latency here. The 25s Flex stall the docs describe did not appear in any of the 21 live calls made during this migration; the slowest was 7.4s.

evidence.detail: Compiled policy applied to a request body: metadata={app,surface}, prompt_cache_key=llmcord.py:on_message, provider_timeout=90.
Live call through llmcord's client with the policy compiled: 200, no 400 for any of the three fields.
Flex vs standard on gpt-6-luna, same prompt: $1.243e-05 (flex, ttft 1.5s) vs $2.266e-05 (service_tier default, ttft 1.9s). Basis for leaving the tier alone.

items.title: Five provider paths keep going to their own providers
items.summary: OpenRouter, Google, xAI, Azure OpenAI and the local servers are not OpenAI hosts, so the runtime leaves them alone.
items.gains: Nothing breaks for anyone whose config.yaml points at these.
items.loses: Their spend stays outside Router: it is not in Router's spend views, it cannot use fallbacks or Flex, and it still needs its own api_key. The shipped `openrouter/~anthropic/claude-opus-latest` entry is in this group twice over -- wrong host, and its model id is not a catalog id, and its openrouter:web_search / web_fetch tools have no Responses equivalent.
items.why: The runtime routes by host and catalog membership. Routing another vendor's OpenAI-compatible host is possible (unlock_hosts) but is a per-operator decision about where spend lands; see i9.

evidence.detail: ROUTER_MIGRATE_TRACE over every model in config.yaml: openrouter.ai -> provider, localhost:11434 -> provider, api.openai.com -> Router.

items.title: Default to gpt-6-luna with reasoning off, and cap reply length
items.summary: Replace gpt-5.5 at reasoning_effort: high as the startup default with gpt-6-luna at effort none, and bound max_completion_tokens.
items.gains: 248x and 348x cheaper per reply on the two side-by-side prompts measured live, and faster to first token (1.4s vs 3.5s), which is what a streaming chat UI is judged on. The output cap closes the only unbounded cost path in the app: nothing stopped a looping model from emitting up to 128k output tokens and splitting them across thirty Discord messages.
items.loses: Real depth on hard questions. gpt-5.5 spent 184-209 output tokens thinking before answering; on a question where that thinking matters, gpt-6-luna at effort none will not match it. gpt-5.5 stays one /model away. The cap can also truncate a genuinely long answer that today would run on.
items.price: gpt-5.5 $5/$30 per 1M -> gpt-6-luna $0.1/$0.5, both Flex-eligible. Measured usage.cost per reply: $0.010681 -> $0.000043 (CRDT explanation), $0.004557 -> $0.000013 (code snippet).
items.why: This is the single largest number in the migration, and it is a product judgement, not a technical one: a snarky Discord bot whose own system prompt says 'Optimize for brevity' was paying for a frontier reasoning model's thinking budget on every @mention. Both models answered the three test prompts correctly and in character. The right default for an interactive chat toy is the cheap fast model, with the expensive one available on request.

evidence.detail: 3 prompts x 2 arms through Router, identical system prompt. Both models correct and in character on all three; gpt-6-luna was more concise.
usage.cost from Router: gpt-5.5 high $0.010681 / $0.004557; gpt-6-luna none $0.000043 / $0.000013.
The new default's exact config (reasoning_effort none + max_completion_tokens 4096) run through llmcord's own client against Router: 200, streamed, finish_reason stop.
2 passed; default model confirmed as openai/gpt-6-luna with its parameters loaded.

items.title: Keep the prompt prefix stable so reply chains hit the cache
items.summary: Send the {date}/{time} lines of the system prompt as a trailing message instead of inside the cacheable prefix.
items.gains: 87% off the input cost of every turn after the first in a conversation, measured. The effect grows with the reply chain: this app allows up to 25 messages of up to 100,000 characters each, all of it behind the system prompt.
items.loses: The model sees the date and time at the end of the conversation rather than inside its instructions. Phrasing that leans on their position ('the line above') would read differently. A system prompt with no {date}/{time} tags is sent exactly as it is today.
items.price: cached input reads at the catalog's cache_read_input rate -- for gpt-6-luna $0.01 against $0.10 per 1M.
items.why: Providers cache on an exact prompt prefix and the system prompt is the prefix. The shipped prompt puts a clock with second resolution in it, so the first bytes of every request differ and nothing behind them can ever be a cache hit. The information is still useful to the model; only its position needs to change.

evidence.detail: gpt-6-luna, a 2.5k-token llmcord-shaped conversation, two turns with different clock values. Clock in the prefix: turn 2 cached 0 of 2578 tokens, $0.000184. Clock at the end: turn 2 cached 2554 of 2582 tokens, $0.000023.

12 assertions driving the real on_message through Discord fakes: the prefix is byte-identical across two turns, the clock still reaches the model and still changes, a tagless prompt is unchanged, a tags-only prompt emits no empty system message. All 12 fail on the pre-change code. Plus the 2 existing tests.

items.title: Tell the user when a reply fails or comes back empty
items.summary: Send one short notice when on_message would otherwise send nothing at all.
items.gains: The bot stops silently ignoring people. Today every exception is logged and swallowed, and a successful call that streams no text does the same; from Discord both look like the bot ignored you, so people @ it again and pay for another call.
items.loses: One extra Discord message on a failed turn.
items.why: This is the worst user-visible behaviour in the app and it costs nothing to fix. It also makes an output cap safe to set: a reasoning model that spends its whole budget thinking returns no text, and without this that turn is silent.

evidence.detail: 6 assertions driving the real on_message: a raising call produces one explanatory reply, an empty stream produces one, a normal answer is untouched and is not replaced by the notice. The three failure assertions fail on the pre-change code.

items.title: Decide image support from the Router catalog, not name tags
items.summary: Use the catalog's input modalities when it knows the model; fall back to the tag list, matched against the model name only.
items.gains: Fixes wrong answers in both directions. gpt-6-luna and deepseek-v4.1-flash take images and matched no tag, so the bot told users 'Can't see images' and dropped their attachments. And 'ollama/mistral-small' matched because 'olLAMA' contains 'llama', so every model served by Ollama, LM Studio or vLLM was treated as a vision model and sent image parts it cannot read.
items.loses: A local model that does see images, is not in the catalog, and is not named with a tag now needs the existing ':vision' suffix (which still forces support on). Previously anything served by Ollama got it for free, by accident.
items.price: no change; marginally cheaper, since images stop being sent to models that cannot read them.
items.why: The migration puts a 73-model catalog with per-model modality data inside the repo. A hand-maintained list of name fragments cannot keep up with it, and the substring match against the provider name was always a bug.

evidence.detail: 14 model keys compared old vs new. Changed: openai/gpt-6-luna False->True, openai/deepseek-v4.1-flash False->True, ollama/mistral-small True->False. Unchanged for gpt-5.5, claude, grok, gemini, gemma, llama4, :vision and the text-only models.

items.title: Fall back across vendors so one outage is not an outage
items.summary: router.policy.json sends a candidate list: the chosen model, then claude-haiku-5-5, then gpt-oss-120b.
items.gains: Three vendors behind every reply (OpenAI, Anthropic, an open-weight host). Router falls through a candidate that errors before generating, so a single-provider incident no longer takes the bot down -- which today means complete silence, since nothing retries and nothing tells the user.
items.loses: When a fallback serves, the reply comes from a model the user did not pick with /model and llmcord does not say which. Fallbacks also only cover failures before the stream starts; Router does not fail over mid-stream. And a models list cannot also carry allow_flex_tier, so the tier Router picks for these requests is less predictable (it served both flex and default across my samples).
items.price: the serving candidate's price, only when it serves. Both fallbacks are cheaper than the default, so this cannot produce a surprise bill.
items.why: A chat bot's failure mode is silence, and llmcord has no retry, no second provider and no user-facing error. Fallbacks are the cheapest availability this app can buy. The runtime's capability guard keeps them honest.

evidence.detail: Compiled-policy expansion: text request -> [gpt-6-luna, claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-oss-120b]; image request -> [gpt-6-luna, claude-haiku-5-5] (text-only gpt-oss dropped by the guard); primary already a candidate -> never duplicated.
Fall-through confirmed: models=[no-such-model-xyz, gpt-6-luna] returned a gpt-6-luna answer, 200, nothing surfaced to the caller. A real llmcord request with the policy compiled: 200, streamed.

items.title: Reuse one OpenAI client per provider, with a bounded timeout
items.summary: Cache the AsyncOpenAI per (base_url, api_key) instead of building one per message, and set a 120s timeout.
items.gains: Drops a TCP + TLS handshake from every single reply, and stops leaking an unclosed httpx connection pool per Discord message in a process that runs for weeks. The timeout replaces the SDK's 600s default, so a provider that accepts the connection and then goes quiet no longer leaves a typing indicator spinning for ten minutes.
items.loses: A client is now built once per provider and key, so it is wrapped for Router once at that moment rather than on every message. If RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY were to appear in the environment after the first message, that provider's existing client would not pick it up until the key or base_url changes. Keys are set at process start in every normal deployment.
items.why: This is the one piece of waste in the hot path that has nothing to do with which model answers. It also makes the Router wrap a one-time cost instead of a per-message one.

evidence.detail: 9 assertions: same provider and key return the same object, a different base_url or a rotated key return a new one (hot reload still works), the timeout is 120s read / 10s connect, the Router transport is installed when the key is set with the real HTTP transport still underneath it, and no Router transport when the key is unset.
The probe routed through get_openai_client still reaches /v1/responses; the client origin is now reported as llmcord.py:get_openai_client.

items.title: Port the call to the Responses API when Router is on
items.summary: Call /v1/responses natively instead of Chat Completions translated by the runtime.
items.gains: Removes the translation layer from the request path. Unlocks the Router fields that policy cannot reach per request: fallback_timeout (stream, two or more candidates -- fail over to a second vendor when the first has not produced a token in N seconds, which is exactly the Flex-stall guard this app wants), a prompt_cache_key per conversation root rather than one for the whole app, max_tool_calls, and the cross-vendor web_search built-in tool. That last one would let the openrouter:web_search entry in config.yaml work on any catalog model instead of only on OpenRouter.
items.loses: A real rewrite of the streaming loop: Responses SSE events are not chat.completion chunks, so the splitting, editing and finish_reason logic in on_message all change, and it would have to stay dual-path because the non-Router providers in config.yaml only speak Chat Completions. Output may differ in small ways. This is the item most likely to introduce a bug, which is why it is proposed rather than built.
items.why: Worth doing only if the operator wants per-request fallback timeouts or cross-vendor web search. The translated path already works and is measurably correct; this buys levers, not correctness.

items.title: Pick the model per message instead of per bot
items.summary: Route short or trivial turns to the cheapest model and reserve a stronger one for long or hard ones.
items.gains: Most Discord turns are a line of banter; a few are real questions. One global /model setting prices every turn at the hardest one. A length-and-keyword heuristic, or Router's own Switchyard model, would cut the cheap turns further without capping the hard ones. With i1 applied the default is already cheap, so the gain here is mostly the ceiling: hard questions could get gpt-5.5 automatically rather than only when an admin remembers to switch.
items.loses: Users lose a single predictable model. The heuristic will be wrong sometimes, and a reply that silently came from a weaker model is hard to debug from Discord. Switchyard ($3/$15) is more expensive than the i1 default, so it only pays if it reliably downshifts.
items.why: The product has one knob (/model, admin-only) for a workload with two very different shapes. Worth measuring before building: a week of logged message lengths would say whether the split is real.

items.title: Opt other OpenAI-compatible providers into Router
items.summary: A per-provider flag in config.yaml that adds that host to the runtime's unlock_hosts.
items.gains: xAI's grok-4.x ids are Router catalog ids, so an operator running x-ai models would get them on one key and one bill with fallbacks and spend labels, without changing a line of their config beyond the flag.
items.loses: Spend moves from that vendor's account to Router, which is a commercial decision, not a technical one. And it costs a wasted round trip per request for BYOK catalog ids: Google's gemini ids are in the catalog but need the caller's own provider credential, so each request would go to Router, come back 403, and only then reach Google. Unlocking generativelanguage.googleapis.com is therefore a bad idea; api.x.ai is a good one.
items.why: Opt-in and off by default, so it changes nothing for anyone who does not set it. Left unbuilt because the default should be chosen by whoever owns the vendor contracts.

items.title: Bound the total size of a reply chain, not just each message
items.summary: Add a whole-conversation character or token budget alongside max_text and max_messages.
items.gains: max_text (100,000 characters) and max_messages (25) multiply out to roughly 600k tokens of input, more than any catalog model's context. A long chain with a couple of pasted files today produces a context-length error, which the app swallows -- so the bot goes quiet exactly when the conversation got interesting. A budget would drop the oldest turns instead and warn, using the warning mechanism that already exists.
items.loses: Older turns silently leave the conversation sooner than max_messages says they will, and the two settings interact in a way that needs documenting.
items.why: Real but less urgent than it looks once i2 lands: cached input makes long chains far cheaper, and i3 at least tells the user something broke. The right budget number depends on the models in use, which is the operator's call.

items.title: Router account settings to confirm on app.router.com
items.summary: Flex default, cross-provider routing and shadow models are account settings, not request fields, and were not changed here.
items.gains: Flex is already on by default for this key and is the right setting for this app: measured -50% cost on gpt-6-luna with no latency penalty. Cross-provider routing and shadow models were not exercised.
items.price: Flex: -50% on Flex-eligible OpenAI models, measured on this key.
items.why: Worth an explicit decision from whoever owns the Router account: keep Flex on (recommended, with evidence); decide whether shadow models are wanted for comparing a cheaper default against the current one on live traffic, which would be a cheap way to validate i1 on real Discord conversations rather than my three prompts.

evidence.detail: gpt-6-luna, same prompt: flex $1.243e-05 at 1.5s to first token; service_tier default $2.266e-05 at 1.9s. Of the 17 live calls in this session that reported a tier, 12 were served at Flex without opting in. Router chooses per request: a plain gpt-6-luna call came back at each tier on different occasions, and a candidate list came back at both.

items.title: Streaming edit cadence is global across conversations
items.summary: last_task_time is one module-level value, so concurrent conversations each reset the other's edit clock.
items.why: EDIT_DELAY_SECONDS is meant to keep Discord message edits to one per second, but last_task_time is shared by every in-flight reply. With several conversations streaming at once, each one sees a time_delta set by somebody else's edit, so the bot edits more often than intended and risks Discord 429s -- which land in the same swallowed exception handler i3 fixes. Not an LLM or Router issue, and not touched here; flagged because it degrades exactly when the bot is busiest.
